title: Flute
reference_instrument: University of Iowa MIS flute (maker and model unstated on the page)
summary: One head-joint pull, nothing retuned per note, leaves D4 at -13.6 c from equal temperament and A5 and G6 at +18.0 and +30.3 c. Every note is too clean, with too little breath noise, and its harmonics miss the recording's. In the scale and melody E5 splits. G4 and C5 start flat. The flute is the printed Pearl PF-661 (Dickens 2007, Listing B.15), hole terms on, slide out 13.2 mm, one set of lengths on every note. The player is one flautist's printed pressure, jet length and lip opening per note (de la Cuadra's thesis); C5 has no printed row and takes the midpoint of B4 and C#5, and G6 takes Fletcher 1975's medians. The jet is computed, a forced Bickley jet driven by the pipe's own sound; A5 speaks in its second register and G6 in its third. The aim was the printed flute and equal temperament, not the recording.
physics_present: The printed Pearl PF-661 flute (Dickens 2007, Listing B.15) as one tone-hole network on every note, with the slide out 13.2 mm, one length for every note, solved once against equal temperament and never against a recording (the only figure printed for this flute at A440 is 8 mm, p. 106)
Printed hole terms on every hole: key cups (eq. 2.30 + 0.1 a, eq. 2.32 where perforated), key pad into closed holes (eq. 5.4), matching length, inner radiation and the series term

One flautist's printed blowing pressure, jet length and lip opening for each note (de la Cuadra thesis Fig. 3.4). D4, G4 and A5 follow that player's printed pressure within the note, then hold its median, and D4 also has the same player's printed breath onset, which G4 and C5 borrow, scaled to each note, because the print has no other. C5 has no printed row: midpoint of B4 and C#5, flat after that start. G6 is past that table: Fletcher 1975's medians over four players, 1254 Pa (band mostly +-50 %) and 4.33 mm (band about +-20 %), with the lip opening and width borrowed from the A5 row, flat after a 50 ms attack

The blow's wander after the printed columns, on the D4, G4 and A5 pages and the scale and melody stops with room for it: its size comes from one player's slurred scale (de la Cuadra 2005 Fig. 3.4, player FA), read off a figure at 8 Pa per pixel, and nothing above about 21 Hz can be seen in that figure
A forced Bickley jet driven by the pipe's own sound, with the Kutta exit and laminar Bickley widening across the mouth

Jet momentum drive (Thwaites and Fletcher 1983, Eq. 1, kappa 1). On the D4 and G6 pages only, it is taken across the jet's own Bickley velocity profile instead of as one lumped flow, which takes 2.0 to 3.1 dB off the term's fundamental there. On G4 and C5 that form takes 2.9 and 3.1 dB off it in the first 0.35 s, and from 0.4 s the note sounds its octave, so those pages keep the lumped term. A C5 render with the lumped term and the station cut width that the profile form brings keeps its register to the release, so the jump is the profile's. A5 keeps its page and the lumped term
The jet's velocity and source term on the embouchure's open strip (hole length x lip opening); the mouth's other terms stay on the mouth area

The jet's swing limit (Fletcher 1976, time form ours) and one jet width in the cut and the swing (Fletcher and Douglas 1980, Verge 1995, Auvray et al. 2014), on the D4, G4, A5 and G6 pages and every note of the scale and melody. C5's own page carries neither row and says why
Breath noise from the turbulent jet (Verge 1995), on above Re_h 700, in a Butterworth band at the cited in-band level

The embouchure radiating from its solved window, under a rigid one-sided lip whose open strip narrows with the note (Coltman via Fletcher 1975), with a rigid half-plane for the player's face just behind the lip's edge

Open holes and the foot radiating through compact baffled loads, summed with the embouchure at a receiver 1.524 m above it on the five note pages: the collection's 5 ft, borrowed, because Iowa's flute page prints no distance and its bassoon and trumpet pages, recorded in the same anechoic chamber with the same Neumann KM 84, print 5 feet. The scale and melody still listen 1 m above it
A warm, moist bore gas from Coltman's measurement on a played flute, with room air outside the instrument
Fractional-delay propagation on every section, and viscothermal loss on the bore sections over a limited band
physics_missing: The right pitch. One pull can't close the spread: D4 is flat at -13.6 c, and A5 and G6 stay sharp at +18.0 and +30.3 c; the momentum drive's profile form brings D4 up 5.7 c and costs G6 5.7 c. Their recordings read -7.5 c and +12.3 c, and G6's is 12 c under it. The stops of the scale and melody play -0.3 to +12.9 c. The pull is 5.2 mm past the only figure printed for this flute at A440, and a flutist would get part of that flattening from the lip and face, which this card doesn't carry. G6 also speaks about 1000 Hz in its first 50 ms and is on the note by 100 ms. From D4 to C5 this flute spreads about 15 c, as the recordings do (16 c), and players on this same flute spread about 24 c (Dickens Fig. 7.2, as we read it). What's left has no printed term we can put on a card: Dickens' eq. 7.2 is fitted to the flutists' pitch, so it isn't used

Harmonics like the recordings'. The largest misses through H8, dB re the first against the recording: D4 H3 -15 against -5, G4 H2 -9 against +2, C5 H2 -21 against -6, A5 H3 -5 against -31, G6 H7 -55 against -25. G4 trades one hole for another: the cut's own second harmonic vanishes when the jet spends half of each cycle on one side and its third when it spends a third, and no render so far has both H2 and H3 right. G4's H3 is that hole. One listening point can swing a single harmonic a long way, because the mouth and the holes can arrive nearly equal and nearly opposite at one point and not at another: between 1 m and 1.524 m above the embouchure, on the same flows, G4's H6 goes from -33 to -15 dB re the first and A5's H3 from -30 to -5, so no one harmonic should be read as the instrument's physics. The receiver sits at the collection's 5 ft, borrowed. There the mean miss over H2 to H12 falls on D4 (8.9 to 7.4 dB) and G4 (10.0 to 6.7) and rises on C5 (5.4 to 6.8) and A5 (5.6 to 7.9)

Breath noise at the right level. Harmonics-to-noise reads above the recording on every note: D4 34.0 against 28.4 dB, G4 36.0 against 30.9, C5 35.9 against 32.3, A5 28.1 against 27.3, G6 37.2 against 22.6. G6's is the largest gap on any flute page; the part we've read is that H1 outgrows the noise. The blow's wander barely touches this. The cards keep the source's level from a recorder-like pipe (Verge 1995), and nothing we found prints a level at this flute's jet length and lip opening, so no gain was set for it

A printed start from rest on any note but D4. G4 and C5 borrow D4's, scaled to each note: the attack comes inside the ruler, but the note starts flat, -24 and -27 c from equal temperament in its first 100 ms, within 5 c of where it holds by about 0.25 s, dipping about twice as far as the recording. Tried on A5, it speaks on A4 for about the first 0.12 s, so A5 keeps its authored 50 ms attack, as do G6 and the scale and melody, whose stops mostly have no room for it

A measured lip jet: the jet's response is computed from a Bickley profile, the jet card on the cards is an estimate (authority X-Est), the labium offset of 0.29 mm is from another player (Onogi), and the mouth contraction of 0.6 was measured on a recorder's mouth (Auvray et al. 2014, Table I), not an embouchure

A printed area for the jet's momentum term. The printed law names the pipe's cross-section and says nothing about a chimney; the cards use the embouchure chimney's area, because on the pipe's area every note we tried jumps toward the octave. Removing the steady momentum part doesn't bring H4 down to the real on any note
The player's real face, lip and lip plate: the lip and face are rigid stand-ins at set positions

Radiation beyond compact baffled loads: the cards' receiver band ends at 2.8 kHz, below the highest harmonics the pages read, the holes sit in a flat baffle plane rather than on the tube, and the openings don't load each other
Viscothermal loss above the cards' band, and any in the hole chimneys or the riser
Wall and pad vibration, vibrato, slurs and tonguing. The scale and melody are one note card per slot, joined, each with its own attack and release
One player's row at G6: its pressure and jet length are medians over four players (Fletcher 1975), and its lip opening and width are A5's

Two notes of the scale and melody don't hold as printed. A4 leaves its note within 3 % of its held 478 Pa, or within 5 % without the pull, both well under the 539 Pa the same player printed on this note, so its 0.5, 0.6 and 1.2 s slots start flat at 478 Pa instead of on the printed track, and this card's first register is narrower than the player's. E5's stop splits: its waveform repeats at half the pitch, with a line at half the pitch 11 dB under the note and lines at 1.5 and 3.5 times the pitch 3 to 5 dB under it
